guide.title: Colonna, Rome: Piazza Colonna, Montecitorio and the seat of government
guide.intro: Colonna is the third of Rome's twenty-two rioni and the one the Italian state works out of. Palazzo Chigi has been the seat of the government since 1961; Palazzo Montecitorio has housed the Camera dei deputati since 1871. Palazzo Chigi stands on Piazza Colonna, which Roma Capitale calls the centre of the city's business and political life. The square takes its name from the Column of Marcus Aurelius standing at its centre, and the rione takes its name from the square. Around that core are a shopping arcade inaugurated in 1922, ten churches, the palace of the Holy See's missionary congregation, and a buried Augustan sundial for which Roma Capitale publishes two addresses in two different rioni. Almost every edge of Colonna is a named street or square, which is why a good deal that visitors file here turns out to sit next door.

sections.heading: The shape of the rione
sections.body:
The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione lists Colonna's five neighbours street by street: Ludovisi along via degli Artisti, via di Sant'Isidoro and via Veneto; Trevi along piazza Barberini, via del Tritone, largo Chigi, piazza Colonna and via del Corso; Pigna along via del Caravita, piazza Sant'Ignazio, piazza San Macuto and via del Seminario; Sant'Eustachio along piazza della Rotonda, via del Pantheon and piazza e via della Maddalena; and Campo Marzio along via di Campo Marzio. Colonna borders neither Parione nor Campitelli. Read that list again and you can see the problem it creates: every one of Colonna's borders is a named public space, so the rione's boundary does not run near piazza Colonna and via del Corso, it runs down them.

That has one consequence worth carrying with you. Where a boundary is defined as a street, mapping data draws the line along one kerb, so the street or square that is the border lands wholly inside whichever side the mapper chose. Buildings are assigned by their own outline; the street they are addressed from is a separate question, and a street address is never a claim about which rione a building is in. This guide follows that rule strictly. Palazzo Fiano is addressed to piazza di San Lorenzo in Lucina, which lies in Campo Marzio, and is nevertheless a Colonna building. Santa Maria Odigitria is addressed on via del Tritone, which the rione article names as part of the Trevi border, and is nevertheless a Colonna church.

It also means several squares get no rione statement here at all. Piazza della Rotonda is a three-rione junction where Colonna, Pigna and Sant'Eustachio meet, and the sources disagree about how many rioni are even involved, so this guide makes no claim on it. Piazza di Spagna, which the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide faces, is in the rione Campo Marzio and is not claimed here either.

Finally, the name trap. The Galleria Colonna and the Palazzo Colonna that appear in guidebooks are the Colonna family's palace and picture gallery, and they are in the rione Trevi, not in the rione Colonna. What Colonna has is the shopping arcade on piazza Colonna, which carried the name Galleria Colonna and which Roma Capitale now publishes as the Galleria Alberto Sordi (già Galleria Colonna). Three names, two buildings, two rioni.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
What follows is the practical information for this rione that could actually be sourced. Almost everything else about getting around Colonna is guesswork, and it is left out.

Two of the buildings can be visited by arrangement. Roma Capitale states that guided visits to Palazzo Chigi, Piazza Colonna 370, are held by prior booking, one Saturday a month from October to June, 9.30 to 13.00, in groups of 35 with entry every thirty minutes, and that booking and the calendar are published by the Presidency of the Council at governo.it/visitare-i-palazzi-istituzionali/visitare-palazzo-chigi/palazzo-chigi-prenotazioni-e-calendario. For Palazzo Montecitorio, Piazza di Monte Citorio 1, Roma Capitale links the Chamber's own visitor site at visita.camera.it and its events site at eventi.camera.it/eventionline. Palazzo Ferrajoli, Piazza Colonna 355, telephone 06 69200497, can be visited only on the occasion of receptions, conferences and exhibitions, per Roma Capitale.

The Galleria d'Arte Moderna di Roma Capitale is at Via Francesco Crispi 24, 00187 Roma, and is part of Roma Capitale's Sistema Musei Civici; entry is free for MIC card holders, and information and booking are on 060608, 9.00 to 19.00. The Museo Missionario di Propaganda Fide, inside the palazzo of the same name, is closed for now: as at 2 September 2026 Roma Capitale states that entry is temporarily closed for urgent conservation work, and its contact is museopropagandafide.va, telephone 06 69880266.

Other addresses, as the institutions give them: Palazzo di Propaganda Fide at Via di Propaganda 1 — not the piazza di Spagna address that circulates, which sends geocoders into the wrong rione; Palazzo Capranica at Piazza Capranica 101 and Via del Collegio Capranica 36-43; Palazzo Wedekind at Piazza Colonna 366; Palazzo Fiano at Piazza di San Lorenzo in Lucina 4; Sant'Andrea delle Fratte at Via di Sant'Andrea delle Fratte 1; the Teatro Sistina at Via Sistina 129; the Teatro Sala Umberto at Via della Mercede 50; Palazzo Marignoli at Via del Corso 180 and Palazzo Bocconi at Via del Corso 189; Santa Maria Odigitria at Via del Tritone 82; and the Orologio di Augusto at Via In Lucina 16/a, which is the Colonna one of the two addresses Roma Capitale gives it.

A warning about hours. No source states opening times for nearly anything in this rione, so nearly none are given here. Roma Capitale's pages for Sant'Andrea delle Fratte, the Teatro Sistina and the Teatro Sala Umberto all say only to contact the church or the venue, so no opening times appear on those records here. Check before you travel.

sections.heading: Where the sources disagree, and what is not claimed
sections.body:
This guide states less than it could, on purpose, and it is worth knowing where the gaps are.

Where two sources of institutional standing give two different figures, no figure is published. That applies to the year the shopping arcade on piazza Colonna was renamed for Alberto Sordi, to the year the Cappella dei Re Magi was built inside Propaganda Fide, and to Giacomo della Porta's birth year, which two Roma Capitale pages give differently. Where a source's own dedicated page for a monument disagrees with its passing mentions elsewhere, the dedicated page is followed: that is why the Column of Marcus Aurelius is dated 180 to 193 here.

Where an institution's map pin disagrees with its own prose, the prose wins. Roma Capitale's page for the church of San Macuto says in words that the church is in the rione Colonna, and its own coordinate for the church falls in the neighbouring rione. The building outline agrees with the prose, so the pin is treated as the error. Objects standing inside piazza della Rotonda are left out of this guide for the mirror-image reason: there the sources pull in opposite directions and nothing resolves them.

Two things in the sources are repeated wrongly often enough to name. Roma Capitale's page on the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide calls the body it houses a Jesuit congregation; the verification behind this guide found that description wrong and it is not repeated here. And the Italian Wikipedia article on the same palazzo files the building under two countries in its infobox and runs two separate articles of the Lateran Treaty together in one sentence. The status of that building is stated on its own record, in the terms the treaty itself uses, and it is not Vatican territory.

There is no shopping or eating in this guide. Colonna has a large commercial layer — dozens of restaurants, hotels, cafés and bars — and none of it could be sourced beyond a mapping database, which is not a source for a guide entry. In particular, no business here is described as historic or long-established: Roma Capitale's register of negozi storici lives on a domain that is unreachable, and a founding date printed in a shop's own name is not evidence of one. Nor does any record on this page make a claim about heritage protection status for any building in the rione: no source states one, so none is given here.

faq.question: What is actually in Colonna?
faq.answer: The political core — Palazzo Chigi, Palazzo Montecitorio, piazza Colonna with the Column of Marcus Aurelius and its fountain, and piazza di Monte Citorio with the Egyptian obelisk. Around it, the Galleria Alberto Sordi arcade, the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide, about ten churches, of which Sant'Andrea delle Fratte, San Macuto and the Santi Bartolomeo e Alessandro dei Bergamaschi rest on Roma Capitale's own pages, a handful of eclectic nineteenth-century palaces along the Corso, two theatres, a civic art museum, and eleven Roman columns embedded in a later building on piazza di Pietra.

faq.question: Can you go inside Palazzo Chigi or Palazzo Montecitorio?
faq.answer: Both by arrangement, neither on a walk-up. Roma Capitale states that guided visits to Palazzo Chigi run by prior booking, one Saturday a month from October to June, 9.30 to 13.00, in groups of 35 with entry every thirty minutes, booked through the Presidency of the Council. For Montecitorio, Roma Capitale points to the Chamber's own visitor site at visita.camera.it. No walk-in access is stated for either.

faq.question: Is the Galleria Colonna in the rione Colonna?
faq.answer: It depends which Galleria Colonna you mean, and it is an easy one to get wrong. The Colonna family's picture gallery and the Palazzo Colonna that contains it are in the rione Trevi. The building in the rione Colonna is the shopping arcade on piazza Colonna, inaugurated in October 1922, which carried the name Galleria Colonna and which Roma Capitale now publishes as the Galleria Alberto Sordi. Three names, two buildings, two rioni.

faq.question: Is piazza di Spagna in Colonna?
faq.answer: No. Piazza di Spagna is in the rione Campo Marzio, even though the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide faces it and is a Colonna building. That is why this guide gives the palazzo the address Roma Capitale gives it, Via di Propaganda 1, rather than an address on the piazza.

faq.question: Is the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide part of the Vatican?
faq.answer: No. It stands in the rione Colonna, on Italian soil, in the Comune di Roma. Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 provides that the building, although forming part of the territory of the Italian State, enjoys the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is not part of Vatican City, it is not Vatican territory, there is no border at its door, and a visitor there is subject to Italian law.

faq.question: Why does this guide leave some squares without a rione?
faq.answer: Because the evidence does not settle them. Several of Colonna's borders are themselves squares and streets, and mapping data draws a boundary along one kerb, so a square that is the border tests as lying wholly inside one side. Where a text source and the geometry disagree, this guide states nothing rather than guessing: piazza della Rotonda is left unresolved. Buildings are assigned by their own outline, so nothing is lost.

photos.title: Piazza Colonna and the Column of Marcus Aurelius
photos.description: The Column of Marcus Aurelius standing at the centre of Piazza Colonna, with Palazzo Wedekind and its portico across the square and Palazzo Chigi, the seat of the Italian government, along the right-hand side.
photos.author: Diego Delso

places.name: Colonna di Marco Aurelio
places.summary: The ancient honorific column standing at the centre of Piazza Colonna, the square that gives the rione its name. Roma Capitale dates the column to between 180, the year of Marcus Aurelius's death, and 193, and records that the work was completed under Commodus, his son and successor. It was inspired by the column of Trajan, rises 100 Roman feet, and stood on a base of 12 metres whose honorific inscription is lost.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the inscription on the base wrongly attributes the column to Antoninus Pius, which is why it has also long been known as the Colonna Antonina. The shaft is wrapped in Carrara white marble reliefs narrating the campaigns against the Germani of 172 and 173 and against the Sarmatians of 174 and 175, the two separated by a figure of Victory, the narrative beginning with the crossing of the Danube on a bridge of boats. Inside, a spiral staircase is lit by slit windows. The reliefs on the base were lost in the restoration of 1589 commissioned by Sixtus V, when a bronze statue of St Paul was placed at the summit.

places.name: Piazza Colonna
places.summary: Roma Capitale calls Piazza Colonna the «centro degli affari e della vita politica della città», the centre of the city's business and political life. Its own description gives the buildings that bound it: Palazzo Chigi, Palazzo Ferrajoli — earlier Del Bufalo, then Aldobrandini, then Niccolini — the small church of the Santi Bartolomeo e Alessandro dei Bergamaschi on the right, Palazzo Wedekind opposite, and behind them the palazzo of the Galleria Colonna, now known as the Galleria Alberto Sordi. The fountain and the column stand at the centre.
places.history: The square is one of the public spaces that the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione names as the line between Colonna and Trevi, which is a caution rather than a contradiction: where a rione boundary is defined as a street or a square, mapping data draws the line along one kerb and the whole space then falls inside whichever side the mapper chose. This guide therefore treats Piazza Colonna as the rione's own square, because the buildings around it are in Colonna, and states no date for when the square was laid out: the sixteenth-century date often attached to it is not on Roma Capitale's page and no other source states it.

places.name: Fontana di Piazza Colonna
places.summary: The fountain at the foot of the column. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that it was made between 1575 and 1577 to a design by Giacomo della Porta and sculpted by Leonardo Sormani, in white marble, portasanta and travertine. Its record gives the rione as Colonna in a field of its own, which is Roma Capitale stating the rione of a monument in its own voice.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza records that della Porta first intended to reuse the first-century river-god statue known as Marforio against a rockwork backdrop beside the base of the column. In the final design the statue was dropped and the fountain was moved away from the column and set parallel to Via del Corso, as an oval portasanta basin with lion-head pilasters in white marble. Its original supply was the Acqua Vergine. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the fountain stands near the aqueduct's main conduit, which was definitively brought back into service under Gregory XIII, feeding the whole Campo Marzio through branches running down from the slopes of the Pincio by way of Via Condotti. In 1830 Achille Stocchi altered the fountain during the repaving of Via del Corso, replacing the central basin and substituting two groups of paired dolphins with intertwined tails inside a shell for the four original water-spouting blocks. It was restored in 1991 and further maintained in 1999. No birth year is given here for Giacomo della Porta: two Roma Capitale pages give two different ones.

places.name: Palazzo Chigi
places.summary: The seat of the Italian government since 1961, on Piazza Colonna. Roma Capitale gives the address as Piazza Colonna 370 and states that guided visits are held by prior booking, one Saturday a month from October to June, 9.30 to 13.00, in groups of 35 with entry every thirty minutes. Booking and the calendar are published by the Presidency of the Council at governo.it/visitare-i-palazzi-istituzionali/visitare-palazzo-chigi/palazzo-chigi-prenotazioni-e-calendario
places.history: Roma Capitale's history of the building begins in the middle of the sixteenth century, when the Aldobrandini commissioned Matteo Bartolini da Città di Castello; Giacomo Della Porta and Maderno are reported on site, but the page says their contribution «non è stato chiarito», has not been clarified. The palace was sold unfinished in 1659 to Mario and Agostino Chigi, brother and nephew of Alexander VII, and completed by Felice Della Greca, who built the courtyard and the Scalone d'onore; the attic was added in the late 1600s. The Piazza Colonna portal, the courtyard fountain carrying the Chigi emblem of six hills beneath a star, and the interior decoration are eighteenth-century, as is the gilding of the Salone d'oro, done for the marriage of Prince Sigismondo Chigi to Maria Flaminia Odescalchi; its ceiling carries Giovan Battista Gaulli, il Baciccia's Endimione spiato da Diana of 1668. The building was earlier a private residence and then the seat of the Spanish and afterwards the Austro-Hungarian embassy to the Quirinal, from which its nickname «mole Austro-vaticana» dates. The State bought it in 1916; it was the Foreign Ministry from 1922 until 1961, when that ministry moved to the Farnesina.

places.name: Palazzo Montecitorio
places.address: Piazza di Monte Citorio 1, Roma RM
places.summary: The seat of the Camera dei deputati, the lower house of the Italian parliament, since 1871. It fronts Piazza di Monte Citorio on one side and Piazza del Parlamento on the other. Roma Capitale gives the address as Piazza di Monte Citorio 1 and links the Chamber's own visitor site at visita.camera.it.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the palace was begun in 1653, when Innocent X commissioned Gian Lorenzo Bernini to build a residence for the Ludovisi, and that work stopped in 1655 at the pope's death for want of funds. It resumed over thirty years later under Innocent XII, with Carlo Fontana modifying Bernini's design while keeping its convex façade and adding the campanile a vela. Innocent XII made it the seat of the Curia Innocenziana, the papal tribunals, inaugurated in 1696; it afterwards housed the Governatorato di Roma and the police directorate. Early in the twentieth century Ernesto Basile built a new block behind the old one, reduced the courtyard, demolished the rear wings and built the floreale front on Piazza del Parlamento, containing the hemicycle chamber lit by Giovanni Beltrami's stained-glass Velario over Giulio Aristide Sartorio's allegorical frieze on the history of the Italian people. The corridor beside the chamber is called the Transatlantico, and the Sala della Lupa is tied to the referendum of 2 June 1946. The great bell, which now rings only on the election of the President of the Republic, once signalled the start of audiences.

places.name: Piazza di Monte Citorio
places.address: Piazza di Monte Citorio, Roma RM
places.summary: The square in front of the Chamber of Deputies, with the Montecitorio obelisk at its centre. Roma Capitale states the rione outright: «la solenne piazza di Monte Citorio si trova nel Rione Colonna».
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the square stands on an artificial rise which some sources attribute to the accumulated rubble of a Roman monument, and that the origin of the name is uncertain. It is variously derived from Citatorius or Saeptorius — citizens having been summoned to the Saepta to elect magistrates since the time of Servius Tullius — or from mons acceptorius, or from a corruption of Monte di Toro.

places.name: Obelisco di Montecitorio
places.address: Piazza di Monte Citorio, Roma RM
places.summary: The Egyptian obelisk in the middle of Piazza di Monte Citorio, also called the Obelisco Campense. Roma Capitale records that it is of the Saitic, twenty-sixth, dynasty, 672 to 525 BC, that it was erected at Heliopolis on the order of Psammetichus II, and that it is of red granite and measures 21.79 metres, or 33.97 metres with its base and globe.
places.history: Brought to Rome under Augustus, it was set up in the Campus Martius on a pedestal bearing the dedication «...AEGYPTO IN POTESTATEM POPULI ROMANI REDACTA SOLI DONUM DEDIT», and Roma Capitale records that it probably served as the gnomon of the sundial whose area at its foot was paved with a representation of the zodiac. It stood until the tenth or eleventh century, then fell, was progressively buried and forgotten. It was found in 1748 broken in five pieces and fire-damaged, recovered under Benedict XIV, and re-erected in its present position in 1792; restored in 1965. In 1998 the piazza was relaid, recreating the zodiacal elements and guide lines that restore its meridian function. The obelisk you see standing is therefore not a thing that has stood here since Augustus.

places.name: Orologio di Augusto
places.summary: A buried Roman monument: a great trapezoidal travertine pavement marking the hours, the seasons, the months and the signs of the zodiac in gilt bronze letters, in the area running from Palazzo Montecitorio to the church of San Lorenzo in Lucina. Roma Capitale publishes two addresses for it in two different rioni — Via In Lucina 16/a in Colonna and Via di Campo Marzio 48 in Campo Marzio — so the monument spans the rione line. This guide carries the Colonna address and makes no claim on the Campo Marzio half.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that it was built in 10 BC, as the inscription at the base of the Montecitorio obelisk — originally its gnomon — records, and that it was positioned so that the gnomon's shadow fell towards the Ara Pacis on Augustus's birthday, 23 September. Excavation in a cellar on Via di Campo Marzio recovered part of the pavement, which Roma Capitale says is perhaps of a later Domitianic phase rather than the Augustan one, with four zodiac names legible in Greek — Virgo, Leo, Taurus and Aries — and the start of Summer. The part that has been recovered is the pavement in that cellar; the monument itself stays buried.

places.name: Palazzo di Propaganda Fide
places.summary: The headquarters of the Holy See's missionary congregation, at the corner where Via di Propaganda meets Piazza di Spagna. The Italian Wikipedia article states twice in its body that the palazzo is in the rione Colonna, and that the block runs between Piazza di Spagna, Via di Propaganda, Via di Capo le Case and Via dei Due Macelli. Roma Capitale gives the address as Via di Propaganda 1, and that is the address used here: the piazza the building faces is in the rione Campo Marzio, and an address on it sends geocoders to the wrong rione.
places.history: The palazzo stands in Colonna, on Italian soil. Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 provides that this building, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is not part of Vatican City, it is not Vatican territory, it is not a border, and a visitor there is subject to Italian law. The Holy See's own list of its extraterritorial properties in Rome names it as entry 5 of 13, «il Palazzo di Propaganda Fide, sede della Congregazione per l'Evangelizzazione dei Popoli». Roma Capitale records that the core of the building dates to 1586 and that it has been the seat of the Congregation De Propaganda Fide, founded by Gregory XV in 1622, since 1633. Between 1642 and 1644 Bernini designed and built the façade towards the piazza for Urban VIII. The façade on Via di Propaganda is Borromini's. The Cappella dei Re Magi inside the palazzo is Borromini's, built after he demolished an earlier elliptical church by Bernini; no construction year is given here, because the two sources reached give different ones.

places.name: Museo Missionario di Propaganda Fide
places.summary: The missionary museum inside the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide. As at 2 September 2026 Roma Capitale states that entry is temporarily closed for urgent conservation work. Museum contact: museopropagandafide.va, tel. 06 69880266.
places.history: Check the museum's own contact before travelling for it. The closure is stated as temporary and no reopening date is stated.

places.name: Galleria Alberto Sordi
places.summary: The covered shopping arcade on Piazza Colonna, which Roma Capitale publishes under the name Galleria Alberto Sordi (già Galleria Colonna). Roma Capitale describes it as Liberty architecture, designed by the Livornese architect Dario Carbone and inaugurated in October 1922, in the period of Rome's transformation into the capital, conceived as a multifunctional block for offices and commerce, and records that it takes its name, as Piazza Colonna does, from the Column of Marcus Aurelius.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the Galleria shut for about a year and reopened in 2024 after a restoration that removed the external glazing and renewed the lighting. The arcade carried the name Galleria Colonna and was later renamed for the actor Alberto Sordi; no year is given here for the renaming, because two institutional sources give two different ones. The Italian Wikipedia article adds that the building is one of the seats of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, that the seventeenth-century palazzo Spada al Corso, later known as palazzo Piombino, stood on the site, and that the work was completed only in 1940 under Giorgio Calza Bini. This is not the Galleria Colonna in the sense of the Colonna family's picture gallery, which is a different building in a different rione.

places.name: Palazzo Capranica
places.summary: A fifteenth-century palace on the square of the same name. Roma Capitale states the rione outright — «il palazzo, sito nell'omonima piazza, all'interno del territorio del rione Colonna, è un edificio del XV secolo» — and gives two addresses for it, Piazza Capranica 101 and Via del Collegio Capranica 36-43.
places.history: The inscription over the portal dates construction to 1451, for Cardinal Domenico Capranica. Roma Capitale records that it was first a Capranica residence and from 1457 a college for clerics. It has a square corner tower whose top storey opens as a loggia, and two marble portals, one reading COLLEGIUM CAPRANICENSE and the other TEATRO CAPRANICA, the second also bearing the date 1451. On the first floor are three Gothic and three Renaissance windows, with traces of the Capranica arms on the Gothic capitals.

places.name: Palazzo Wedekind
places.summary: A palace on Piazza Colonna, also called the Palazzo del Tempo, fronted by a portico of sixteen columns. Roma Capitale records that twelve of those columns came from the excavations of the Etruscan city of Veio, as the Latin frieze inscription states.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the palace was built from the second half of the 1600s and owes its present appearance to the nineteenth-century restorations of Pietro Camporese and Giovanni Battista Giovenale, commissioned first by Gregory XVI and then by the Wedekind family. It was the papal postal office, then briefly the Education Ministry of the Kingdom of Italy; the banker Karl Wedekind bought it in 1879; it passed to INPS in 1925; it was the official seat of the Fascist Party from 1943 to the liberation of Rome, and later the home of the newspaper Il Tempo. Inside are the Sala Giovenale, with decorated ceilings and Renaissance-inspired mosaic floors designed by Giovenale in 1881, a second salone with a seventeenth-century tapestry from the Sciarra Collection, and a collection of about ninety twentieth-century works.

places.name: Palazzo Ferrajoli
places.summary: A palace on Piazza Colonna, its façade of four storeys divided into three by four rusticated vertical bands. Roma Capitale states that it can be visited only on the occasion of receptions, conferences and exhibitions, and gives the telephone number 06 69200497.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that it was built over the old houses of the Del Bufalo-Cancellieri and that in the 1500s its façades were partly frescoed; that it was modernised in 1561 by Giacomo Della Porta and restructured in 1626 by Francesco Peparelli, which gave it its present appearance, for the marriage of Paolo Del Bufalo to a Santacroce. It passed to the Niccolini in 1728. Cardinal Joseph Fesch, Napoleon's uncle and French ambassador to Rome, was installed here under the Empire, and the Marchese Giuseppe Ferrajoli bought it in 1850.

places.name: Palazzo Fiano al Corso
places.address: Piazza di San Lorenzo in Lucina 4, Roma RM
places.summary: A palace addressed to Piazza di San Lorenzo in Lucina. The piazza it is addressed to lies in the rione Campo Marzio; the palazzo itself is not a straddler and is a Colonna building. Roma Capitale records that the first remains of the Ara Pacis were found here during the excavation works of 1568.
places.history: Roma Capitale records a thirteenth-century core, wholly rebuilt in the 1400s as the residence of the titular cardinals of San Lorenzo in Lucina; it passed to the Peretti, the family of Sixtus V, around the mid-1600s, and to the Dukes Ottoboni di Fiano in the 1800s, whence the name. Edoardo Almagià bought it in 1898. It was the seat of the Circolo degli scacchi from 1923 to 1990. The salone was frescoed in the mid-1600s by Giovan Francesco Grimaldi and François Perrier, with an adjoining Sala degli Specchi.

places.name: Palazzo Capranica Macchi di Cellere
places.address: Piazza di Monte Citorio, Roma RM
places.summary: A palace on Piazza di Monte Citorio. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna. No source states more.
places.history: Roma Capitale publishes no page for this palace and no other source states it.

places.name: Palazzo Marignoli
places.summary: An eclectic palace filling a whole block, addressed at Via del Corso 180. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna and describes the block as running between Piazza di San Silvestro and Via del Corso, bounded by Via delle Convertite and Via di San Claudio.
places.history: No source states more than its identity, its rione and its street.

places.name: Palazzo Bocconi
places.summary: An eclectic palace on Largo Chigi, addressed at Via del Corso 189. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna.
places.history: Two dates for the building circulate and they cannot both be right, so neither is given. Its later commercial tenancies are likewise not stated, because no source states them.

places.name: Palazzo delle Poste a Piazza di San Silvestro
places.address: Piazza di San Silvestro, Roma RM
places.summary: The post office building on Piazza di San Silvestro. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna, on the block bounded by Via del Moretto, Via della Vite and Via del Gambero, the same block as the church of San Silvestro in Capite, and records that it houses the post office Roma V.R., frazionario 55001.
places.history: No source states more than its identity, its rione and its street.

places.name: Palazzo Chauvet
places.address: Via dei Due Macelli, Roma RM
places.summary: An eclectic palace on Via dei Due Macelli. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna. No source states more.
places.history: Roma Capitale publishes no page for this palace and no other source states it.

places.name: Palazzo Gabrielli-Borromeo
places.address: Piazza di San Macuto, Roma RM
places.summary: The palace adjoining the church of San Macuto, now the Jesuits' Collegio San Roberto Bellarmino. Roma Capitale's page on the church records the adjoining college and its earlier name as Palazzo Gabrielli-Borromeo.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the church of San Macuto has been part of the Collegio Bellarmino since 1942.

places.name: Collegio dei Bergamaschi
places.summary: A palace at the corner of Via di Pietra and Via dei Bergamaschi. The Italian Wikipedia article places it explicitly in the rione Colonna.
places.history: No source states more than its identity, its rione and its street.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Andrea delle Fratte
places.address: Via di Sant'Andrea delle Fratte 1, Roma RM
places.summary: A church with an apse, a dome drum and a campanile by Borromini. Roma Capitale records it from the twelfth century as Sant'Andrea «infra hortos», later rendered «delle Fratte», and gives the address as Via di Sant'Andrea delle Fratte 1. Its official site is madonnadelmiracolo.it. Roma Capitale publishes no opening hours for it and says only to contact the church, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Sixtus V entrusted the church to the Order of Minims of St Francis of Paola in 1585 and that they began the rebuilding, funded by the Marchese Ottavio del Bufalo, whose buffalo-head arms appear on the portal pediment and on the campanile. The work dragged on for over a century for want of funds. The general design and the façade are Gaspare Guerra's, who worked there from 1604 to 1612; in 1653 the commission passed to Borromini, who designed the apse, the campanile and the dome drum, the dome left unfinished at his death, and Mattia de Rossi finished the work in 1691. The campanile is nicknamed «ballerino», the dancer, because the structure sways alarmingly when the great bell rings, and the diagonal buttresses of the tiburio make the form of St Andrew's cross. The Italian Wikipedia article adds that the church received the title of minor basilica on 25 April 1942, that it is called the santuario della Madonna del Miracolo after the Ratisbonne apparition of 20 January 1842 — a title corroborated by the official domain Roma Capitale itself lists — and that Maximilian Kolbe said his first Mass here on 29 April 1918.

places.name: Chiesa di San Macuto
places.address: Piazza di San Macuto, Roma RM
places.summary: A church dedicated to the Breton bishop Machutus, on the square of the same name, adjoining the Collegio San Roberto Bellarmino. Roma Capitale states the rione in words: «si trova sulla piazza omonima a Roma, nel rione Colonna».
places.history: Roma Capitale records the church from 1192; it was under San Marcello al Corso in the later thirteenth century, then under the Dominicans of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, confirmed by Nicholas III in 1279, and was a parish church by 1422. In 1516 Leo X united the parish to the Chapter of St Peter's, which ceded it to the Confraternita dei Bergamaschi in 1539 — two separate events that are often merged into one. A new façade was built about 1560 by Giovanni Alberto de Galvani, and the church was partly rebuilt between 1577 and 1585 to Francesco Capriani da Volterra's design. The parish was suppressed in 1588. The Bergamaschi left for Santa Maria della Pietà in 1725-26 and the Jesuits took the church back under the San Macuto title; it has been part of the Collegio Bellarmino since 1942. One data caution: the map pin on Roma Capitale's own page for this church falls outside the rione its own prose gives. The prose and the building outline agree on Colonna and the pin is the outlier.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Bartolomeo e Alessandro dei Bergamaschi
places.summary: A small church on Piazza Colonna — Roma Capitale's description of the square places it to the right — also known as Santa Maria della Pietà. Roma Capitale records that it was founded in 1561 as the chapel of the adjoining Ospedale dei Pazzi.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page on San Macuto records that the Bergamasque confraternity moved here in 1725-26 and that the title changed to the Santi Bartolomeo e Alessandro. The Italian Wikipedia article describes it as the national church of the Bergamaschi in Rome.

places.name: Basilica di San Lorenzo in Lucina
places.address: Piazza di San Lorenzo in Lucina, Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica in the rione Colonna, on the piazza of the same name.
places.history: Roma Capitale publishes no page for this basilica and no source states more than its identity and its location.

places.name: Chiesa di San Silvestro in Capite
places.address: Piazza di San Silvestro, Roma RM
places.summary: A church on Piazza di San Silvestro. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna.
places.history: No source states more than its identity and its location.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Maddalena
places.summary: A church on the square of the same name. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna. A name trap worth knowing: mapping data calls it Santa Maria Maddalena in Campo Marzio, but that epithet is the ancient Campus Martius, not the modern rione Campo Marzio.
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article records that the church has a rococo interior, that it holds the remains of St Camillus de Lellis, and that it is the regional church of the Abruzzesi in Rome. No institutional page states it, so those three facts rest on that article alone.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria in Aquiro
places.summary: A church on Piazza Capranica. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna.
places.history: No source states more than its identity and its location.

places.name: Chiesa di San Giuseppe a Capo le Case
places.summary: A church in the rione Colonna. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione; no street number for it was found in any source reached, so none is given.
places.history: No source states more than its identity and its rione.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Ildefonso e Tommaso da Villanova
places.summary: A church on Via Sistina. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna, in via Sistina.
places.history: The same article records that the church holds an Adorazione dei pastori by Francesco Grassia of 1670. No institutional page states it, so that rests on the article alone.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Odigitria
places.summary: A church on Via del Tritone, also called Santa Maria dell'Itria. The Italian Wikipedia article places it in the rione Colonna, at number 82 of via del Tritone, and describes it as the national church of the Sicilians in Rome.
places.history: Worth knowing if you are checking the address against a map: the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione names via del Tritone as part of the Colonna/Trevi border, and a street address is not a claim about the rione of the building on it.

places.name: Teatro Sistina
places.summary: A theatre on Via Sistina. Roma Capitale records that it was inaugurated in 1949 as a cinema-theatre to a design by Marcello Piacentini, and that the culture ministry recognised it as Teatro stabile della Commedia Musicale Italiana in March 2003. Roma Capitale publishes no hours and says to contact the venue, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that its popularity owed above all to Garinei e Giovannini, whose works were staged in over 45 countries and translated into 16 languages, and that Massimo Romeo Piparo has directed it since July 2013, succeeding Gianmario Longoni.

places.name: Teatro Sala Umberto
places.summary: A theatre on Via della Mercede. Roma Capitale records that it was designed by Andrea Busiri Vici, with decoration by the scenographer Alessandro Bazzani, and opened in 1882 as a concert hall named the Teatro della Piccola Borsa.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Giulio Podesti enlarged it to 650 seats in 1890, that it was renamed around 1900 and used as a Cinemofono from 1906, and that Petrolini debuted here on 25 May 1911. Attilio Spaccarelli and Arnaldo Foschini refitted it for the Universal Exposition marking fifty years of Italian unity, the work finished in 1913, and it was rebuilt in 1928 with a twelve-metre proscenium and modern projection equipment. Roma Capitale describes it as a temple of variety and revue between the 1910s and the 1940s.

places.name: Galleria d'Arte Moderna di Roma Capitale
places.summary: A civic art museum on Via Francesco Crispi, part of Roma Capitale's Sistema Musei Civici. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which runs it, writes: «Nata nel 1925, la collezione custodita nella Galleria di Via Crispi documenta l'ambiente artistico romano tra la seconda metà dell'Ottocento e il secondo dopoguerra» — founded in 1925, the collection documents the Roman artistic world between the second half of the nineteenth century and the years after the Second World War.
places.history: Entry is free for MIC card holders. Information and booking are on 060608, 9.00 to 19.00.

places.name: Tempio di Adriano (Hadrianeum)
places.summary: Eleven columns of a Roman temple, embedded in a later building on Piazza di Pietra, and later in use as the Borsa di Roma, the city's stock exchange. No institutional page for the temple exists on Roma Capitale's site, so what is stated here is the identity of the building and nothing else.
places.history: One trap to know before you read about it elsewhere. The Italian Wikipedia article describes the temple as «sito nel Campo Marzio», which means the ancient Campus Martius and not the modern rione Campo Marzio. The same epithet sits inside the mapped name of the church of Santa Maria Maddalena, which is also a Colonna building.

entries.name: Piazza Colonna
entries.note: Palazzo Chigi, Palazzo Ferrajoli and Palazzo Wedekind stand around it, with the fountain and the column at the centre.

entries.name: Colonna di Marco Aurelio
entries.note: Dated 180 to 193 and completed under Commodus, its marble reliefs narrate the Danube crossing and the campaigns against the Germani and the Sarmatians.

entries.name: Fontana di Piazza Colonna
entries.note: Made 1575 to 1577 to Giacomo della Porta's design and sculpted by Leonardo Sormani; Achille Stocchi put in the paired dolphins in 1830.

entries.name: Palazzo Chigi
entries.note: Seat of the Italian government since 1961; guided visits run by prior booking, one Saturday a month from October to June, in groups of 35.

entries.name: Palazzo Montecitorio
entries.note: Begun 1653 to Bernini's design and finished by Carlo Fontana; the Camera dei deputati has sat here since 1871 and visits go through the Chamber's own site.

entries.name: Obelisco di Montecitorio
entries.note: Raised at Heliopolis under Psammetichus II, found broken in five pieces in 1748 and re-erected here in 1792; the 1998 repaving restored its zodiac and meridian lines.

entries.name: Palazzo di Propaganda Fide
entries.note: Bernini built the front towards the piazza between 1642 and 1644 and Borromini the one on Via di Propaganda; the building stands on Italian soil, not Vatican territory.

entries.name: Galleria Alberto Sordi
entries.note: Dario Carbone's Liberty arcade, inaugurated in October 1922 and reopened in 2024 after a restoration that removed the external glazing.

entries.name: Palazzo Wedekind
entries.note: Its portico carries sixteen columns, twelve of them brought from the excavations of Veio, as the Latin frieze inscription states.

entries.name: Basilica di Sant'Andrea delle Fratte
entries.note: Borromini designed the apse, the dome drum and the campanile nicknamed «ballerino», which sways when the great bell rings; contact the church for hours.

entries.name: Tempio di Adriano (Hadrianeum)
entries.note: Eleven Roman columns stand embedded in the later building on Piazza di Pietra, which afterwards served as the city's stock exchange.

entries.name: Galleria d'Arte Moderna di Roma Capitale
entries.note: The civic collection formed in 1925, covering Roman art from the later nineteenth century to the years after the Second World War; free with the MIC card.

entries.name: Teatro Sistina
entries.note: Inaugurated in 1949 as a cinema-theatre to Marcello Piacentini's design, and tied to the musicals of Garinei e Giovannini; contact the venue for what is on.
